name: Tatta adavu (floor strikes)
summary: The first adavu: hold aramandi and strike the floor with the flat of the foot, alternating, in time.
setup: Face the phone about 2.5 m away, camera at hip height. Sit into aramandi and hold it. Lift one foot a few centimetres and strike the floor flat, sole slapping down as one piece, then the other. Count in fours.
brief: Sit into aramandi and hold it. Lift one foot a few centimetres and strike the floor flat, the sole slapping down as one piece, then the other.
why: The foot lifting and striking is a clear up-and-down the camera can count from the front. Whether the strike actually sounded, and whether the sole landed flat, it cannot hear or see.
calibrationPose: Held in aramandi, both feet flat, before the first strike.
tempo: Start slow — one strike per second. Speed comes later.
progression: Double and quadruple speed; then the same in muzhumandi.
regression: Stand tall instead of in aramandi; strike more slowly.
contraindications: Heel or knee pain that builds; a hard floor without a mat if the joints are sensitive.

faults.label: Standing up out of the stance
faults.tip: The stance is held the whole time. Rising with each strike is the commonest way beginners save their thighs.

faults.label: Striking with the toes or heel first
faults.tip: The sound comes from the whole foot landing at once. Toe-first is a different adavu and a sore foot.

faults.label: Lifting the foot too high
faults.tip: A high lift breaks the rhythm and the stance. The foot barely leaves the floor.

faults.label: Chasing the speed
faults.tip: Uneven strikes at speed are worth less than even ones slowly. Match a beat you can hold.

faults.label: Arms drifting
faults.tip: The hands stay where the teacher placed them; drifting arms are a sign the legs are struggling.

guide.surface: Wooden or hard floor, barefoot. A thin mat if the joints are sensitive; never a thick carpet.
guide.stop: Pain in the heel, shin or knee that builds through the set.
guide.cannotSee: Whether the strike made a clean sound, and whether the sole landed flat.

points.t: Aramandi held throughout — the body does not rise between strikes.
Spine vertical, tailbone tucked, shoulders down.
The foot lifts only a few centimetres and lands as one flat piece.
The standing foot stays completely still.
Hands at the waist in kati hastam, elbows lifted and still.
